ABSTRACT
The exchange of data among Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) devices belonging to dif-
ferent organizations is a crucial element for fully exploiting the technological potential of
Industry 4.0 and for consolidating this ecosystem. Despite technological advances, signifi-
cant obstacles related to interoperability and, especially, to the sharing and control of data
between entities that do not maintain a prior relationship of trust still persist. In particular,
there is difficulty in establishing mechanisms that allow granular control of access to in-
formation, while simultaneously ensuring privacy, auditability, and transparency of sharing
rules. Traditional solutions tend to depend on centralized intermediaries or implicit trust
models, which limits their application in multi-organizational industrial environments. In
this context, this dissertation investigates an approach to enable the secure exchange of data
in distributed IIoT environments, combining message-oriented communication mechanisms
with distributed ledger technologies and cryptographic techniques. The proposal explores
the use of smart contracts on the Hyperledger Besu blockchain to formalize, manage, and
audit access permissions, as well as the application of Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE)
to ensure that shared data is accessible only to entities that meet predefined access policies.
The developed architecture reduces the dependence on unilateral control over access rules
by recording governance-related information on blockchain, while ABE enforces data con-
fidentiality outside the chain. By combining these mechanisms, the solution supports secure
and auditable data sharing among organizations, enabling scenarios such as real-time trac-
king in supply chains and privacy-preserving industrial data exchange, thereby contributing
to the digital transformation of organizations and to the advancement of Industry 4.0.
Keywords: Industrial IoT, Blockchain, Data Privacy, Interoperability, Attribute-Based Encryption.

Chapter 1
INTRODUCTION
The growth of Industry 4.0 has driven a structural change in manufacturing, characterized
by the integration of cyber-physical systems, automation, and digital technologies in industrial
environments. The authors Kagermann et al. (2013) describe Industry 4.0 as the deep integration
of physical production systems with digital infrastructures, enabling interconnected and data-
driven industrial processes.
The conceptual origin of the termIndustrial Internetis commonly associated with Evans
& Annunziata (2012), who described the convergence of industrial machines, advanced com-
puting, data analytics, low-cost sensing, and Internet connectivity as a new wave of industrial
innovation. In this context, the expressionIndustrial Internet of Things(IIoT) emerged as a
specific designation for the application of IoT principles within industrial environments. To es-
tablish a formal baseline, this work adopts the definition provided by Industrial Internet Consor-
tium (2017), which characterizes IIoT as a set of interconnected industrial systems and devices
capable of collecting and exchanging data to support monitoring and automation.
Since IIoT environments are based on the interconnection of industrial systems and the
exchange of operational data, interoperability becomes a central concern. However, interopera-
bility is a multidimensional concept. The European Interoperability Framework (EIF) organizes
interoperability into technical, semantic, organizational, and legal layers (European Commis-
sion, 2017). ISO 11354-1, published by the International Organization for Standardization
(ISO), in turn, structures enterprise interoperability according to aspects such as business, pro-
cesses, services, and data, as well as conceptual, technological, and organizational barriers
(ISO, 2011). Thus, interoperability does not refer only to the exchange of messages between
systems, but also to the ability of different entities to coordinate processes, interpret data, and
govern interactions across organizational boundaries.
In this dissertation, interoperability is addressed within a restricted scope. The work fo-
cuses on technical interoperability, supported by publish/subscribe communication based on

1.1 Motivation 14
MQTT, and, primarily, on governance- and security-oriented interoperability, aimed at enabling
data exchange between independent administrative domains without presupposing a prior trust
relationship. Semantic interoperability, including the harmonization of sensor data models and
the interpretation of heterogeneous measurements and distinct physical phenomena, is outside
the scope of this research.
Recent forecasts indicate that the global number of IoT-connected devices will reach 29
billion by 2030 (ABUSERRIEH; ALALFI, 2024). However, the rapid expansion of industrial
systems also intensifies challenges related to secure cross-organizational data sharing, inclu-
ding technical connectivity, access governance, privacy, and auditability (HAZRA et al., 2021).
In these scenarios, there is generally a need for real-time data exchange to support decision-
making, while each organization maintains its own governance structures, information mana-
gement flows, and confidentiality requirements. These factors can restrict inter-organizational
collaboration, especially when sensitive operational information must be shared without com-
promising confidentiality and integrity.
The strategic sharing of information may enable new business models, but it also contrasts
with the risk of undue data exposure. Therefore, these conditions require mechanisms capa-
ble of enforcing secure and manageable data sharing between different organizations, while
preserving the ability of each party to define, enforce, and audit its own access rules.
To illustrate this situation, consider a supply-chain scenario involving a sensor manufactu-
rer, an automobile manufacturer, and a maintenance service provider. The maintenance provider
may require access to operational data to perform predictive maintenance services. At the same
time, the automobile manufacturer may need to restrict production metrics, while the sensor
supplier may protect proprietary device configurations. This scenario shows that organizations
may need to share data selectively while remaining administratively independent and without
relying on a single trusted intermediary.
This need for data sharing between organizations can be supported by mechanisms that
ensure granular access control over shared data, without requiring all parties to depend on a
single centralized authority.
1.1 Motivation
As highlighted by Mahendran et al. (2025), the lack of mechanisms for secure cross-
organizational IIoT data sharing, coupled with the need for access governance and auditabi-
lity, remains a significant challenge in Industry 4.0, especially among segregated organizations.

1.1 Motivation 15
Nishi et al. (2024) also emphasize that IoT sensor networks based on standardized architectures
such as IEEE P1451.1.6, a smart transducer network standard that facilitates interoperability in
distributed systems, still face persistent problems related to secure authentication, trust mana-
gement, and integration across distinct environments.
Where devices operate under different administrative domains and governance policies,
these challenges intensify. Beyond operational limitations, this gap compromises data consis-
tency and reliability, important requirements for feasibility analysis of different data-driven ap-
proaches and potential Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications. Traditional IIoT security archi-
tectures rely on centralized communication models based on MQTT brokers, static Access Con-
trol Lists (ACLs), Transport Layer Security (TLS) authentication, and public key infrastructure-
based mechanisms. However, these approaches have limitations in inter-organizational environ-
ments where different entities need to share data while preserving granular and dynamic privacy
policies. Hamad et al. (2023) explain that MQTT publish/subscribe architectures are inheren-
tly dependent on centralized brokers and that their respective TLS-based protection methods
primarily protect communication channels but do not meet end-to-end, data-centric protection
requirements for the payload itself. As a result, intermediate components, such as brokers, can
still access or manage sensitive information during message routing.
Furthermore, Xu et al. (2018) argue that traditional access control approaches, including
ACL and RBAC-based models, face scalability and management limitations in ecosystems com-
posed of multiple administrative domains. As highlighted by the authors, the obstacles related
to maintaining authorization rules arise as the number of devices, organizations, and access
relationships increases. This limitation is particularly relevant in interoperable IIoT scenarios,
where different companies may operate under independent governance policies.
To address these challenges, Rasori et al. (2022) describe Attribute-Based Encryption as
a data-centric security mechanism capable of incorporating granular access control policies
directly into encrypted data. The authors emphasize that this approach reduces reliance on
centralized trust models and allows for the secure sharing of information even in distributed
or partially untrusted environments, making ABE suitable for applications requiring granular
privacy preservation.
In addition to interoperability challenges, data security and privacy remain central concerns
in IIoT environments. The distributed and interconnected nature of these environments increa-
ses their exposure to cyber threats. According to Check Point Research, cyberattacks targeting
industrial IoT devices increased by 45% in 2024 compared with the previous year, exposing in-
dustries to risks such as data breaches, unauthorized access, and operational disruptions (Check
